title: How I made Unity MCP’s tool overhead 25× smaller without removing a single operation
author: Complex-Chance-7258
selftext:
I use AI agents with Unity a lot, and one thing kept driving me crazy: a huge part of the context window was disappearing before the model had even touched the scene.

In my baseline measurement, the regular Unity MCP exposed 48 tools with 93,119 characters of serialized schemas.

Using the usual characters-to-tokens approximation, that is roughly 23,280 tokens of tool definitions. Not scene data. Not code. Just the instructions describing what the tools can do.

Then the agent would inspect a large hierarchy, read a noisy console trace, or receive a giant generic response containing fields it did not need. More context was consumed, the model became less focused, and simple Unity tasks started requiring far too many round trips.

I had already spent a lot of time optimizing MCP workflows while working on [MCP Hub](https://github.com/Vangardo/mcp_hub) and a similar Blender setup. The same pattern kept appearing:

The model rarely needs the entire API surface at once.

It needs a very small, predictable interface, a good way to find the correct operation, and compact results that can be expanded only when necessary.

So I built **Unity MCP Efficient**:

[https://github.com/Vangardo/unity-mcp-efficient](https://github.com/Vangardo/unity-mcp-efficient)

It does not replace or fork MCP for Unity. The original Unity MCP still performs the actual work. This is a thin facade and Codex skill placed in front of it.

Instead of exposing dozens of large tool schemas to the model, the facade exposes six small tools:

* Search for the relevant Unity capability
* Inspect only the required operation schema
* Execute a single operation
* Batch multiple operations
* Inspect Unity in a compact form
* Retrieve or expand stored results when needed

Underneath those six tools, 377 Unity operations remain available.

Here are the current measured results:

|Measurement|Original surface|Efficient facade|Reduction|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|Exposed MCP tools|48|6|87.5%|
|Serialized schema size|93,119 chars|3,657 chars|96.07%|
|Approximate schema tokens|23,280|915|96.07%|
|Argument fields presented through schemas|5,566|1,798|67.7%|
|Large synthetic hierarchy response|628,110 chars|875 chars|99.86%|

The included search evaluation currently finds the expected Unity operation at rank one for all 15 tested intents.

The hierarchy number is deliberately a stress test, not an average scene. Also, the 96% figure refers specifically to the exposed tool-schema surface. I am not claiming that every Unity session will become exactly 96% cheaper. Actual savings depend on the model, task, caching and how much scene data is requested.

A few less visible problems also needed fixing:

* Large raw results are stored before compaction, so the model can retrieve details later without repeating the Unity operation.
* FastMCP and Pydantic response objects are normalized safely instead of failing during JSON serialization.
* Async test jobs preserve their `job_id`.
* Inner Unity failures cannot incorrectly appear as an outer `ok: true`.
* Domain reloads, stale editor state and temporarily missing Unity sessions return compact retry guidance.
* Related operations can be sent through bounded batch calls instead of spending a full model round trip on every small action.
* Scene inspection prefers summaries, component counts and grouped information instead of dumping every vertex or hierarchy field by default.

The project currently has 35 automated tests, CI across Python 3.10–3.13, reproducible benchmark scripts, an MIT license and installation instructions for Codex.

I built this because I wanted Unity agents to spend their context on reasoning about the game, not repeatedly reading thousands of tokens of API documentation.

If you already use MCP for Unity, I would genuinely appreciate real projects that can break this approach. Huge scenes, ProBuilder workflows, noisy consoles, long test runs and painful domain reload cases are especially useful.

Repository:

[https://github.com/Vangardo/unity-mcp-efficient](https://github.com/Vangardo/unity-mcp-efficient)

Benchmarks and methodology:

[https://github.com/Vangardo/unity-mcp-efficient/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md](https://github.com/Vangardo/unity-mcp-efficient/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md)

comments.author: lorendroll
comments.body: Exactly what I wanted to find today for my local agent! Will give it a try, thanks.

comments.author: Lord-Fondlemaid
comments.body: FYI Unity MCP is being retired soon(ish) and replaced by Unity CLI. I'm just testing it out now, going well so far! Check their news (and your email which is how they told me)

replies.author: Complex-Chance-7258
replies.body: Cool. I hope they pull it off right. There are some issues at the moment, though. Still, my skill goes a long way. At least the token cost is lower and the execution is faster.

replies.author: Lord-Fondlemaid
replies.body: I found Unity MCP a bit flaky with Codex... it would keep dropping connection/becoming invisible. Codex couldn't properly diagnose why, and I definitely wouldn't have been able to!

replies.author: Complex-Chance-7258
replies.body: It's possible. But I rarely had any problems.

replies.author: YellowMerigold
replies.body: You mean the official Unity CLI? If yes, how does it work with Codex? Unity MCP is easy to install and used through Codex.

replies.author: Lord-Fondlemaid
replies.body:
I'll paste the email I got below:

Hello,
 
Following the positive reception of the new Unity CLI, and mixed feedback with the current Beta in-Editor MCP server, we are announcing the deprecation of the MCP server in the AI Assistant package.
 
The new CLI and its MCP mode will replace the in-editor MCP server. It brings several benefits:
Dramatically faster iteration times by using the Roslyn compiler for evaluating code, avoiding editor recompiles and domain reloads
Drastically improved stability
Use your own AI Agent (Claude, Codex, etc) with 0 configuration
Ability to target runtime, not just the Editor!
Implement custom commands in an easier way
A broader set of commands and tools available to agents
An MCP mode to replace the in-Editor MCP server
A set of public Skills ready for your agent to use
The MCP Server in the AI Assistant package will continue to be supported at least until the end of 2026. We will communicate an official schedule at a later time.
 
What you need to do when you're ready. Install the CLI, add the pipeline package to your project, and point your agent at it. See our Documentation.
 
We and our community of Beta users truly believe that the Unity CLI defines a new standard on how we create games in tandem with AI Agents, and we are excited to see how far our users can push it!

More info on the Unity website.

replies.author: YellowMerigold
replies.body: Thank you, much appreciated! Time to dig through Unity's CLI documentation.
